title: A nil pointer in an error is not nil
claim: find returns a nil pointer, so err == nil is true.
why: An interface value holds a type and a value. err holds the type *MyErr and a nil pointer. Only an interface with no type at all equals nil, so the check is false.

title: Two appends, one backing array
claim: b and c are separate slices, so b[3] is 1 and c[3] is 2.
why: a has room for one more element. Both appends write into that same spare slot of the same backing array, so the second append overwrites the first.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := make([]int, 3, 4)
	b := append(a, 1)
	c := append(a, 2)
	fmt.Println(b[3], c[3])
}

title: Appending to a sub-slice changes the original
claim: b is a new slice, so appending to it leaves a alone.
why: b := a[:2] shares a's array and still has capacity 3. append writes 99 into index 2, which is a[2].

title: A slice of a slice is a window, not a copy
claim: part is a copy of two elements, so orig is unchanged.
why: Slicing makes a new slice header that points into the same array. Writing part[0] writes orig[1].

title: Arrays are copied, slices are not
claim: b := a shares the array, so a[0] becomes 99 too.
why: An array is a value. Assigning it copies all three elements. A slice would have shared them.

title: range gives you a copy of each element
claim: The loop adds 10 to every player's score.
why: p is a copy of each element. Changing p changes the copy. Use players[i].Score += 10 to change the slice.

title: Reading a struct from a map copies it
claim: p is the struct inside the map, so m["a"].X becomes 100.
why: Map values are copied out when you read them. p is a separate struct; the map still holds the old one.

title: A value receiver changes a copy
claim: Inc runs twice, so n is 2.
why: Inc has a value receiver, so each call gets its own copy of the Counter. Use func (c *Counter) Inc() to change the original.

title: defer evaluates its arguments right away
claim: The deferred print runs last, so it prints 2.
why: The call runs later, but its arguments are evaluated when the defer statement runs. x was 1 at that moment.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 1
	defer fmt.Println("deferred:", x)
	x = 2
	fmt.Println("now:", x)
}

title: Deferred calls run in reverse
claim: The defers print 0, 1, 2.
why: Deferred calls are pushed on a stack and run last-in, first-out when the function returns.

title: Closures in a loop (Go 1.22 changed this)
claim: Every closure sees the last value of i, so it prints 3 3 3.
why: That was true before Go 1.22. Since 1.22 each iteration has its own i, so each closure captures a different variable and it prints 0 1 2.

title: := in an inner block makes a new variable
claim: The if block changes x to 3.
why: x := 2 declares a new x that only lives inside the block. The outer x is never touched.

title: Integers wrap around silently
claim: Adding 1 to 127 gives 128, or a panic.
why: int8 holds -128 to 127. Going past the top wraps to the bottom. Go does not check for overflow at run time.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var x int8 = 127
	x++
	fmt.Println(x)
}

title: Integer division truncates toward zero
claim: -7/2 rounds down to -4.
why: Go integer division truncates toward zero, so -7/2 is -3. The remainder takes the sign of the left operand.

title: 0.1 + 0.2 depends on where you add it
claim: Both sums print the same number.
why: Constants are exact, so 0.1 + 0.2 is exactly 0.3 at compile time. Variables are float64, and the binary values of 0.1 and 0.2 do not add up to exactly 0.3.

title: len counts bytes, not letters
claim: "héllo" has 5 letters, so len is 5 and s[1] is é.
why: Strings are bytes. é takes two bytes in UTF-8, so len is 6, and s[1] is the first byte of é (195).

title: range over a string jumps by bytes
claim: The indexes are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
why: range decodes one rune at a time and gives its byte offset. é is two bytes, so the index jumps from 1 to 3.

title: A nil slice and an empty slice are different
claim: Both are empty, so both equal nil.
why: var a []int has no backing array, so it is nil. []int{} has one with length 0, so it is not nil. Both have len 0 and both work with append.

title: copy stops at the shorter slice
claim: copy grows dst to fit all three values.
why: copy never allocates. It copies min(len(dst), len(src)) elements and returns that count.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	dst := make([]int, 2)
	n := copy(dst, []int{1, 2, 3})
	fmt.Println(n, dst)
}

title: Receiving from a closed channel never blocks
claim: The second receive blocks forever or panics.
why: After close, receives first drain the buffer, then return the zero value at once with ok == false.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan int, 1)
	ch <- 5
	close(ch)
	a, ok1 := <-ch
	b, ok2 := <-ch
	fmt.Println(a, ok1, b, ok2)
}

title: switch stops after one case, unless you say fallthrough
claim: fallthrough checks the next case's condition first.
why: fallthrough jumps straight into the next case body without checking it. So "two" prints even though the value is 1.

title: Returning a pointer to a local is safe
claim: n dies when newCounter returns, so the pointer dangles.
why: Go sees that &n outlives the call and allocates n on the heap. Watch it move on the stage. The garbage collector frees it when nothing points to it.

title: Reading a nil map works, writing panics
claim: A nil map is just empty, so writing to it is fine.
why: A nil map has no storage. Reads return the zero value, but a write has nowhere to go and panics. Create it with make first.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var m map[string]int
	fmt.Println(m["x"])
	m["x"] = 1
	fmt.Println("unreachable")
}

title: An unbuffered send needs a receiver
claim: The send stores 1 in the channel, then the receive reads it.
why: An unbuffered channel has no room. The send waits for a receiver, but the only receiver is the next line of the same goroutine. Every goroutine is asleep, so the runtime stops with a deadlock.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan int)
	ch <- 1
	fmt.Println(<-ch)
}
